background.definition: Menopause: a natural process, not a disease; cessation of ovarian function, confirmed by 12 months of amenorrhea following the final menstrual period (FMP). Perimenopause (also called menopausal transition): period of time in which the first endocrine, biological, and clinical features of approaching menopause begin, up through 1 year after the FMP. Vasomotor symptoms (VMS): hot flashes and night sweats; caused by falling or fluctuating estrogen levels, usually beginning around the time of perimenopause. Genitourinary symptoms of menopause (GSM, formerly “atrophic vaginitis” or “vulvovaginal atrophy”): vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary tract dysfunction and recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI) due to thinning of tissue of the lower genitourinary tract caused by estrogen deprivation. Estrogen: naturally occurring estrogens include estrone (E1—weaker, predominates after menopause), 17-estradiol (E2—most potent, predominates during reproductive years, but significantly decreased after menopause, most common therapeutic form), and estriol (E3). Synthetic estrogen esters (longer duration of action) include estradiol acetate, estradiol benzoate, estradiol cypionate, and estradiol valerate. Conjugated equine estrogens (CEE) are less commonly used than in the past. Esterified estrogens (EE) are synthetic plant-based estrogens. Ethinyl estradiol is commonly used in oral contraceptives. Progestogen: includes progesterone (predominant naturally occurring progestogen) and progestins (synthetic progestogens— medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA), levonorgestrel, norethindrone). Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT): treatment of patients during or following menopause with one of several estrogen formulations, with or without a progestogen, by any one of several routes, for a variety of indications. Estrogen therapy (ET): estrogen-only therapy, no progestogen, for patients without a uterus. (Endometrial protection is not needed.) Estrogen–progestogen therapy (EPT): combined estrogen–progestogen, for patients with an intact uterus. (Endometrial protection is needed.)

list.listitem: More than 50 million menopausal women by the year 2020 in the United States. About 1.3 million women in the US experience menopause annually.
Menopause usually occurs between age 47 and 55 years (mean age 51–52 years).

VMS which are moderate or severe affect about 50% of midlife women. VMS last a median of 7.4 years; however, one-third of women may have moderate or severe VMS for >10 years. African-American race, obesity, anxiety, and younger age at symptom onset are associated with a greater risk of more severe VMS.
Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) affects most women to some degree, with moderate or severe symptoms in about 20% to 45% of women, with varying rates of progression.

The increased rates of cardiovascular disease, cognitive problem and dementia, Parkinson’s disease, osteoporosis, mood disorders, anxiety, other mental health concerns, and sexual dysfunction seen in midlife women are thought to be at least partially related to the physiologic changes of menopause rather than solely due to normal aging (see also “Pathophysiology”).

There may be an increased risk of stroke with earlier menopause onset, although data are inconsistent. Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 cohort studies found a higher risk of heart failure and atrial fibrillation among women who had undergone early menopause compared with women who had undergone menopause after age 45 years (HR 1.2, 95 % CI 1.1-1.4; HR 1.1, 95 % CI 1.04-1.1, respectively).
The overall prevalence of sleep disorders among postmenopausal women was 51.6% (95% CI 44.6-58.5%) based on a meta-analysis.

Use of MHT was associated with a lower relapse risk among women with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder for those age 40-49 years (adjusted Hazard Ratio [aHR] 0.86, 95% CI 0.78-0.95) and age 50-55 years (aHR 0.74, 95% CI 0.66-0.83) when compared to non-use, but not for women aged 56-62 years.
Loss of ovarian follicular function, leading to falling estrogen levels, and reflected by elevated gonadotropin levels.
Menopause may also be precipitated by oophorectomy, chemotherapy, or radiation therapy (iatrogenic).
Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) may be worsened by medications (e.g., aromatase inhibitors, tamoxifen) or radiation.
During perimenopause, there is erratic ovarian follicle maturation with fluctuating estrogen and progesterone levels and rising serum FSH levels.
Vasomotor symptoms (VMS) are related to estrogen withdrawal and pulsatile pituitary luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion, which triggers release of various neurotransmitters.
Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) is directly related to decreased estrogen levels over time.
There is some evidence for a direct association between estrogen and various disturbances of mood and cognition.

Mood and anxiety disturbances may be related to perimenopausal hormone changes, although primary mood and sleep disorders are also more prevalent in this age group. Childhood adversity also appears to accelerate early onset of menopause (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.2-1.9).
Concentration difficulties and forgetfulness may be related to perimenopausal hormone changes, but also to sleep disturbances or normal aging.
Decreased libido and sexual dysfunction may be related to perimenopausal hormone changes, but perhaps are more directly linked to sleep disturbances or to the vaginal dryness of GSM.

While increases in fat mass in women are primarily attributed to aging, authors of a meta-analysis suggest that the observed decrease in total leg fat percentage and increase in central fat are indicative of a possible change in fat mass distribution after menopause, likely due to the higher testosterone to estradiol ratio, which has been linked to enhanced central adiposity deposition.

Investigators using posttrial analysis of data from the Early vs Late Intervention Trial with Estradiol found opposite effects of plasma estradiol levels on atherosclerosis progression, as measured by carotid artery intima-media thickness (CMIT), based on the timing of initiation of MHT. Among women beginning MHT within 6 years of menopause, higher E2 level was inversely associated with CIMT progression and in those initiating MHT 10 or more years after menopause, E2 level was positively associated with CIMT progression.

VMS following oophorectomy are generally more severe and prolonged. Oophorectomy is also associated with an increased risk of osteoporosis with a faster rate of bone loss, as well as a significantly greater progression of carotid artery intima–media thickness.
It is unclear if diet is associated with time of onset of menopause.

The USPSTF (2022) updated their 2017 recommendations and once again determined that the magnitude of both benefits and harms of menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) in postmenopausal women is small to moderate. Therefore, they recommend against use of combined estrogen and progestin for primary prevention of chronic conditions based on moderate certainty of no net benefit.

Based on pooled data from 3 prospective cardiovascular disease cohorts including 2,917 postmenopausal women with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes mellitus, ever use of MHT was associated with reduced risk of stroke (hazard ratio[HR] 0.86, 95% CI 0.76-0.98), coronary heart disease (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.74-0.98), and atherosclerotic heart disease (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73-0.95) in white but not black women. Findings were similar for early (within 5 years) initiation of MHT.

Assist patients through education and preparation about the menopause transition, postmenopausal health, and evidence-based treatment recommendations. Many midlife women are uncertain and apprehensive about menopausal symptoms and treatment options. Consider initiating discussions about menopause and MHT any time after age 40 years; many patients wish to discuss this topic before the onset of menopause.

Inquire about vasomotor symptoms (VMS), genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), mood and concentration issues, and sexual dysfunction. Since the publication of the initial Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) trial data in 2002, women and their providers have faced significant questions and concerns about MHT, and many women may not ask about, much less request treatment for, troublesome menopausal symptoms.
Suspect perimenopause based on age and symptoms (see “Definition” and “Prevalence”); diagnostic tests are usually not needed.
Tests for FSH or estradiol may be helpful in women with apparent menopausal symptoms who are younger than age 40 years or who are still having regular menses.
Evaluate apparent flushing and sweating if associated with fever, weight loss, localized pain, cough, or diarrhea.
Evaluate new-onset symptoms in previously asymptomatic postmenopausal women.

list.listitem: Suspect perimenopause based on age and symptoms.
Individual symptoms are not very helpful diagnostically; VMS have the greatest positive predictive value (LR+ 2.2).

VMS: sudden sensation of heat in face, neck, and chest, persisting for several seconds to minutes; may also include flushing, chills, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and palpitations. Authors of a systematic review note that measures used to assess menopausal VMS in clinical trials vary greatly and that standardized measures are needed.

In a study of 2,016 women enrolled in Kaiser Permanente Northern California health care system, current symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder, reported by 22.5%, were associated with VMS (OR 1.69; 95% CI 1.34-2.12), night sweats (OR 1.72; 95% CI 1.37-2.15), and vaginal dryness (OR 1.73; 95% CI 1.37-2.18). Women with a lifetime history of intimate partner emotional (21%) or physical (15.7%) violence also had a higher risk of night sweats (OR 1.5 and 1.33, respectively).

Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM): vaginal dryness, irritation or itching, burning, dyspareunia, urinary urgency or frequency, with thinning of labia majora and resorption of labia minora, pale/shiny/dry vulvar and vaginal mucosa; may progress in severity.
Diagnostic tests are not usually needed. Serum FSH does not correlate with intensity or frequency of hot flashes.

For women with menopausal symptoms but who are less than age 40 years and/or still having menses, testing (FSH and estradiol) is recommended to confirm the diagnosis. Elevated FSH and decreased estradiol support the diagnosis. Inhibin A and B are sometimes used, but are not more accurate than FSH.For women on cyclic oral contraceptives, check FSH no sooner than day 5-7 of the hormone-free interval.
If a genitourinary syndrome of menopause diagnosis is uncertain: consider tests to rule out infection (bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, candidiasis), UTI, and malignancy.
There is insufficient evidence regarding salivary hormone testing for diagnosis, treatment, or monitoring of menopause.
Suspect menopause in women with menopausal symptoms and/or irregular/absent menses.
In women with menopausal symptoms who are less than age 40 years and/or having menses, order FSH and estradiol (E2) to confirm the diagnosis.

Consider menopause as a contributing factor in women with mood or anxiety symptoms, sleep disturbances, or concentration difficulties and forgetfulness. Also consider asking about intimate partner violence in women reporting VMS, night sweats, and vaginal symptoms.

Consider use of a model of empowerment when counseling women about the menopause transition. This approach goes beyond symptom management to support women in an active process of gaining knowledge, confidence, and self-determination to self-manage their health and make informed decisions about care.
Menopausal hormone therapy appears to be underused among women with early or surgically-induced menopause, which may lead to excess morbidity and mortality.
A significant number of women with moderate to severe menopausal symptoms could benefit from menopausal hormone therapy (MHT); systemic MHT is the most effective treatment for VMS.
Low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy is the most effective treatment for genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM).

In younger women (within the first 5–10 years of menopausal transition, less than age 60 years) with vasomotor symptoms (VMS) who do not have any excess risk for breast cancer or cardiovascular disease (CVD), the benefits of MHT may outweigh its very small absolute risks.

Women with an intact uterus should be prescribed EPT to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Women with a hysterectomy do not need a progestogen and may be prescribed estrogen-only therapy (ET).
Women receiving only low-dose vaginal estrogen do not need a progestogen even if they have an intact uterus.
Many patients have troublesome menopause symptoms for a decade or longer; it is generally safe to continue MHT at whatever dose and for however long is necessary.
Consider natural oral progesterone rather than synthetic progestins and intermittent use of progestogen to minimize breast cancer risk.

Several non-hormonal treatments may also be helpful for menopausal symptoms, including neurokinan inhibitors, although they are not as effective as MHT. Some have not been evaluated in clinical trials.

listitem.strong: Decision-making about menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) in early menopause

list.listitem: Patient selection: In symptomatic younger women (within the first 5–10 years of menopausal transition, less than age 60 years) who do not have any excess risk for breast cancer or cardiovascular disease, the benefits of MHT generally outweigh its very small absolute risks. Women with troublesome menopausal symptoms may be unnecessarily forgoing effective relief due to overestimating risks and lack of familiarity with treatment options both by themselves and by their providers.

Duration of treatment: While some guidelines discuss continued MHT in terms of “lowest dose for the shortest time,” this is based on very weak evidence. Many women have menopausal symptoms for a decade or longer, and for women who are appropriately selected, benefits of ongoing MHT may outweigh risks.

Shared decision-making: Individualize treatment based on clinical factors, patient preference, and shared decision-making. Before initiating MHT, screen for any increased breast cancer or coronary heart disease (CHD) risk. Help each woman decide how important the potential risks and benefits are to her unique situation. (A Menopause Decision-Support Algorithm and companion MenoPro iPhone/iPad app are available to help clinicians advise women about their various options as well as risks and benefits of MHT.)

Systemic MHT vs low-dose vaginal estrogen: “Systemic” MHT refers to estrogens and progestogens administered via oral, transdermal, and certain vaginal routes and at doses sufficient to cause systemic effects (both positive and negative) and to impact risks of therapy. Low-dose vaginal estrogen preparations result in very small, if any, increases in serum estrogen levels and, although they may have some systemic effects, for the most part they do not carry the risks associated with systemic MHT.

Emerging information and better understanding: Since the publication of the initial Women’s Health Initiative trial data in 2002, patients and their providers have faced significant questions and concerns about MHT. Although no adequately powered RCTs have been conducted with symptomatic women in early menopause, updated subgroup analyses have provided a better understanding of the factors affecting risks and benefits in women ages 50 to 59 years. These results apply only to MHT using CEE with or without MPA, and cannot be extrapolated to other regimens. However, there is evidence that these data provide the most conservative, “worst-case” estimates. “Critical window hypothesis”: Among various studies, some seem to show a protective benefit of MHT against CHD while others seem to demonstrate an increased risk. The reason for this discrepancy remains controversial, but many authorities suggest that estrogen started earlier provides a measure of protection against the development of CHD, while estrogen started later, after disease has become established, can provide little if any benefit. In addition, in older women benefit is further outweighed by the thromboembolic risks of estrogen, particularly oral estrogen (see also below).

Transdermal vs oral estrogen: Because of the thromboembolic risk of oral estrogen, transdermal estrogens (including systemic formulations of intravaginal estrogens), which avoid “first-pass” metabolism in the liver, are preferred over oral estrogens in current clinical practice. Transdermal estrogen preparations are more expensive than oral preparations, and some women at low risk for CVD may choose oral estrogens based on lower cost or preference. Either transdermal or oral estrogen (plus progestogen for women with an intact uterus) are the treatments most likely to reduce the frequency of vasomotor symptoms among menopausal women.

Progestogen effects: In many instances, the reported risks and benefits of MHT are related to progestogen rather than estrogen. For instance, breast cancer risk is increased with EPT, but much less so with ET, and while ET may be cardioprotective, EPT is not. Conversely, while unopposed estrogen in women with an intact uterus increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, EPT largely eliminates this concern.
Potential Benefits of menopausal hormone therapy (MHT)

Vasomotor symptoms (VMS) are most effectively treated with systemic MHT, with a 75% reduction in hot flush frequency (95% CI 64.3–82.3) relative to placebo. Interestingly, the estimated change of VMS frequency in placebo arms of 17 studies evaluated was -5.44 times per day (95% CI -5.81 to -5.07 times per day) at week 12. For VMS severity, the estimated change with placebo at week 12 was -0.36 (95% CI, -0.46 to -0.27), based on data from 13 studies.

genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) is a progressive condition of varying severity among menopausal women. Low-dose vaginal estrogen is the preferred treatment for symptoms of GSM including urinary incontinence and recurrent UTI. Authors of a systematic review found vaginal estrogen may improve vulvovaginal dryness, dyspareunia, most bothersome symptom, and increase treatment satisfaction although most trials were of short duration and used varying definitions of GSM. Systemic MHT is usually effective, but additional vaginal estrogen may occasionally be required.

Osteoporosis: MHT is effective for osteoporosis prevention and treatment, and for reducing fracture risk for women in early menopause and may be considered first-line therapy in women ages 50 to 59 years. This benefit continues during treatment but decreases after treatment stops, although it may persist longer in women who have taken MHT for more than 10 years. Benefit on hip and vertebral fracture prevention is also seen in older women on combined MHT. Fracture prevention has only been demonstrated for oral CEE with or without MPA, although transdermal estradiol has been shown to improve bone density. Other agents are equally effective, and in current clinical practice, MHT is less commonly used solely for this purpose.

The American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and American College of Physicians guidelines recommend alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid, and denosumab as the first-line of therapy for women with osteoporosis (see Osteoporosis). The newest guidelines from the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada recommend use of anabolic agents (romosozumab or teriparatide) for up to one year as first-line therapy in patients with osteoporosis at high risk of an imminent fracture followed by 5 or more years of bisphosphonate therapy.
Mood and anxiety disturbances, as well as difficulties with concentration and forgetfulness, may be effectively treated with systemic MHT, although this is not always predictable.

In a RCT of 172 women aged 45 to 60 years who were medically healthy and euthymic at study enrollment, clinically significant depressive symptoms developed in fewer women assigned to cyclic HT than to the placebo control group (17.3% vs 32.3%; number needed to treat = 6.6; 95% CI 3.6–46.5).

Sleep disturbance: Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 studies found MHT improved self-reported sleep outcomes (standard mean difference [SMD] -0.13, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.08, I2 = 41), but not sleep parameters measured by polysomnography. Transdermal administration was more beneficial than oral and EPT had a positive effect on sleep while ET did not.

Cardiovascular disease: There is mixed evidence for a small cardioprotective benefit of ET started within the first 10 years of menopause. A 2025 Cochrane review concluded neither ET nor EPT, when used for at least a year, affected the risk of CVD. This was an update to a previous Cochrane review (2015) that found a reduced risk of mortality (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.52–0.95, moderate quality evidence) and death from cardiovascular causes and non-fatal myocardial infarction (RR 0.52; 95% CI 0.29–0.96, moderate quality evidence). The older review found the effect may not be observed until after 5 to 6 years of treatment and is not seen with EPT. Both studies concluded long-term use of MHT for CVD prevention cannot be recommended.

Dementia and cognition: The evidence with regard to a protective benefit against dementia from MHT is also mixed. While ET started early in the menopause may confer a modest benefit, this effect is not immediately observed and may not be seen with EPT. See Risk section below.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies with 2,818 participants found no effect of MHT on verbal memory in postmenopausal women, regardless of time of initiation, and may impair some domains of short-term memory.

Sexual function: MHT is associated with a small to moderate improvement in sexual function when used specifically in women with menopausal symptoms or who were in early postmenopause (within 5 years after the onset of menopause), but not when used for any postmenopausal woman.

Evidence regarding other HTs (tibolone, raloxifene, and bazedoxifene) is of low quality. Current evidence does not suggest an important effect of tibolone, raloxifene and bazedoxifene, alone or combined with estrogens, on sexual function.

The Endocrine Society guideline recommends against use of testosterone for women with sexual dysfunction other than hypoactive sexual desire disorder. Potential adverse effects include increased hair growth, acne, and decreased HDL cholesterol.

Weight gain and body fat distribution: There is no evidence that ET or EPT have an effect (neither promoting nor preventing) on body weight or the BMI increase normally seen following menopause. No statistically significant difference was found in mean weight gain between those using unopposed estrogen and non-MHT users (0.03 kg; 95% CI −0.61 to 0.67) and those using estrogen with progestogen therapy and non-MHT users (0.04 kg; 95% CI −0.42 to 0.50). There was no significant difference in BMI between women using unopposed estrogen and non-MHT users (−0.14 kg; 95% CI −0.40 to 0.12) or estrogen combined with progestogen and non-MHT users (−0.10 kg; 95% CI −0.27 to 0.07). Insufficient data were available to enable meta-analysis of the effect of HRT on waist-to-hip ratio, fat mass, or skinfold thickness.

Mortality: MHT, in both primary and secondary prevention trials, does NOT reduce all-cause mortality. A recent meta-analysis found no effect on mortality (RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.94–1.05), regardless of MHT type or history of preexisting heart disease. No association was found between MHT and cardiac death (RR 1.04; 95% CI 0.87–1.23) or stroke (RR 1.49; 95% CI 0.95–2.31). Investigators found no overall mortality benefit from MHT in a population-based prospective cohort study in Denmark of 29,243 women with a median follow up of 17.6 years.

EPT use was associated with a likely increase in breast cancer mortality (RR 1.96; 95% CI 0.98–3.94), whereas ET use was not. MHT use was not associated with mortality of other types of cancer. In five trials, MHT was likely started at a younger age: two RCTs with mean age less than 60 years and three RCTs with MHT started less than 10 years after menopause. Meta-analysis of these five RCTs showed a reduction of mortality with MHT (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.52–0.95).
Potential Harms of MHT (see also )

In younger women (within the first 5–10 years of menopausal transition, less than age 60 years) who do not have any excess risk for breast cancer or CVD, the benefits of MHT may outweigh its very small absolute risks (breast cancer and VTEs being of greatest concern).

VTE: Oral MHT increases the risk of both deep venous thrombosis (CEE: 3/1000 per 5 years, HR 1.66 (0.76–3.67), CEE+MPA: 6/1000 per 5 years, HR 3.01 (1.36–6.66)) and pulmonary embolism (CEE: 2/1000 per 5 years, HR 1.53 (0.63–3.75), CEE+MPA: 3/1000 per 5 years, HR 1.53 (0.63–3.75)).

In contrast, while observational studies have consistently suggested that transdermal estrogen does not increase VTE risk, the existing evidence is inadequate to demonstrate this effect. In a recent UK nested case-control study of women aged 40-79 years, exposure to MHT within 90 days prior to the index date occurred in 5795 (7.2%) of women diagnosed with VTE compared to 21,670 (5.5%) of control women. Increased risk was only seen with use of oral and not transdermal estrogen.

Some forms of progestogens, but not all, may also influence risk. One meta-analysis concluded that in spite of low-quality evidence, a strong recommendation for non-oral routes of ET, particularly for women with increased VTE risk, is justified.

Breast cancer: There is a small increased risk of breast cancer of approximately 1–2 excess cases/1000 women per year with EPT. This risk was seen only with synthetic progestins (e.g., medroxyprogesterone acetate) but not with oral micronized progesterone. Vaginal estrogen appear safe even among women with prior breast cancer.

In a meta-analysis of worldwide epidemiologic data, investigators found excess breast cancer risk with every MHT type, except vaginal estrogens; risk increased steadily with duration of use and was greater for estrogen-progestogen than estrogen-only preparations. Among current users, adjusted risk ratio (RR) during years 1-4 for estrogen-progestogen was 1.6 (95% CI 1.5-1.7) and for estrogen-only RR was 1.2 (1.1-1.3). During years 5-14, risks were higher (estrogen-progestagen RR 2.1 [1.02-2.2] and estrogen-only RR 1.3 [1.28-1.37]). Even after stopping MHT, excess risk persisted for more than 10 years, although there was little excess risk if MHT duration was <1 year. For women with 5 years of MHT use starting at age 50 years, this translates into an increased incidence of breast cancer at ages 50-69 years of about one in 50 among estrogen plus daily progestogen preparation users, one in 70 among estrogen plus intermittent progestogen preparation users, and one in 200 users of estrogen-only preparations. These risks double with use of MHT for 10 or more years.

Gallbladder disease: The risk of symptomatic gallbladder disease in menopausal women on MHT is approximately doubled after 5 to 7 years of use, but the absolute risk is small, increasing from 2.5/1000 women to 4.5/1000 women.

Endometrial cancer: While use of ET in women with an intact uterus increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, the standard clinical practice of EPT largely eliminates this concern. A 2025 Cochrane review noted there was little evidence beyond 1 year of follow up for the risk of endometrial hyperplasia with EPT, and insufficient evidence to determine the risk of endometrial cancer. Adequate progestogen regimens include micronized progesterone 100 mg per day continuously or 200 mg per day for 10 to 14 days sequentially each month or levonorgestrel-releasing IUD. Higher doses of progestogen may be required when higher doses of estradiol are used or in women with obesity.

Stroke: Based on many systematic reviews, MHT may increase stroke risk. Cochrane authors estimated the risk at 6/1000 women (NNTH = 165, mean length of follow-up: 4.21 years [range: 2.0–7.1]). Stroke risk was most evident for women initiating MHT >10 years from menopause (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.06–1.38). Compared to oral estrogen, transdermal estrogen does not appear to increase stroke risk.

Urinary incontinence: While local estrogen treatment may be beneficial, urinary incontinence may be worsened with systemic MHT using CEE, with both estrogen-only (RR 1.3; 95% CI 1.2–1.5) and CEE combined with progestin (RR 1.1; 95% CI 1.04–1.2).

Dementia: Although evidence with regard to MHT influence on dementia is mixed, in a 2019 Finnish national databases study of 84,739 women diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and 84,739 age- and hospital district-matched control women, use of systemic MHT was associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease of between 9% and 17%. The risk did not differ significantly for those on estrogen-only vs. combined estrogen-progestogen therapy (OR 1.09; 95% CI 1.05-1.14 and OR 1.17; 95% CI 1.13–1.21, respectively).

Using data from a nationwide, nested case-control study in Denmark including 5589 incident cases of dementia and 55,890 age-matched controls aged 50-60 years, authors found an increased risk of all-cause dementia in those receiving combined estrogen-progestogen therapy (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.3), with increasing durations of use yielding higher hazard ratios.
Authors of a 2021 meta-analysis of 23 RCTs found that MHT negatively affects global cognition, especially after 60 years of age and more than 6 months of therapy

Systemic MHT is the most effective treatment for VMS, with 75% to 90% reduction in frequency of hot flashes and night sweats (progestogen needed in women with intact uterus—see below).

Standard doses:
Estradiol, transdermal: 0.0375 to 0.075 mg per day Estradiol, oral: 1 mg once daily Conjugated equine estrogens (CEE): 0.625 mg once daily

Higher doses (oophorectomy, earlier menopause):
Estradiol, transdermal: 0.1 mg per day (or greater) Estradiol, oral: 2 mg once daily Conjugated equine estrogens (CEE): 1.25 to 2.5 mg once daily

Oral progestins, used alone without estrogen, can also be used to treat hot flashes; the best studied is MPA, 10 to 20 mg daily. Topical progestins, in the form of progesterone cream,may be effective for vasomotor symptoms (but are not effective for endometrial protection).

Other medications may also be helpful for menopausal symptoms, although not as effective as MHT, or have not been evaluated in clinical trials. (MHT is about 90% effective and the best non-hormonal therapies are 40%−50% effective, about equal to low-dose systemic estrogen—placebo typically considered to be 30% effective.)

Authors of a recent systematic review and meta-analysis found that selective serotonin receptor inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) were not likely to be beneficial and were more likely to be discontinued than placebo. However, in a recent RCT including 91 Mexican patients, those randomized to citalopram reported a significant improvement in Menopause Rating Scale scores compared to fluoxetine as well as improvement in psychological and somatic domains at 3 and 6 months of follow-up.
Other options include gabapentin 900 to 2400 mg total daily dose and clonidine; the latter is modestly more effective than placebo but used infrequently due to side effects.

In a phase 3 placebo-controlled RCT including 2205 patients, fezolinetant, a neurokinin 3 receptor antagonist, at 30 mg and 45 mg doses significantly reduced the severity of vasomotor symptoms at weeks 4 and 12 over placebo. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 65 (37%) of 174 women in the fezolinetant 30 mg group, 75 (43%) of 173 in the fezolinetant 45 mg group, and 78 (45%) of 175 in the placebo group.

Using pooled data from 1022 women aged 40 to 65 years with moderate-to-severe VMS, fezolinetant treatment was associated with improvement in overall quality of life, measured by reduction in MENQoL score, and work productivity. This was also confirmed in a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs showing improved quality of life as well as lower VMS frequency (pooled mean difference 2.6, 95% CI 1.8-3.4).

Fezolinetant was also found to be effective in a randomized trial of women with moderate-to-severe VMS who did not want hormones or had a contraindication to hormonal therapy. The rate of VMS symptoms decreased from 10.6 per day at baseline to 2.61 per day in the treatment group compared with 4.67 in the placebo group (p<0.001).

A phase 3 RCT evaluated the effectiveness of elinzanetant, a NK1/NK3 inhibitor, at a dose of 120mg daily. Participants had a baseline of 6.7 VMS episodes daily and were randomized to the active medication or matched placebo; they were followed for 52 weeks. The primary outcome was number of moderate to severe VMS events, and it decreased more in the active group (-5.4 vs -3.4). Adverse effects included somnolence, fatigue, and headache and were more common in the active treatment group (30% vs 14.6%).
Elinzanetant was also found to be effective at reducing VMS in patients with symptoms due to endocrine therapy for breast cancer, such as tamoxifen.

Placebo effect can be substantial; in VMS trials, authors of a meta-analysis of 17 and 13 studies, respectively, found a reduction of 5.44 times per day in frequency and 0.36 in severity observed as a placebo effect.

Low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy has been considered to be the most effective treatment for GSM; type of estrogen does not matter (progestogen not needed—see below). Up to 20% of women on systemic MHT may still need additional vaginal estrogen for more complete relief of GSM symptoms. One vaginal estrogen product is an estradiol acetate ring (Femring) that delivers a systemic dose of estrogen. This product is approved for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms in addition to vulvar and vaginal atrophy (VVA). Femring should not be confused with Estring, which delivers a low dose of estrogen and is indicated only for VVA. Options include: Estradiol, intravaginal cream, ring, or tablet: 10 to 25 mcg twice weekly (Estring: estradiol 7.5 mcg/d, Vagifem: estradiol 10 mcg twice weekly) CEE. Intravaginal cream: 0.3 mg twice weekly Estrogen intravaginal ring: changed every 3 months Estrogen cream: 0.5 mg twice weekly

Acceptability of the vaginal ring was evaluated in a meta-analysis of 50 studies with 19,271 ring users; results showed a favorable acceptability pooled prevalence of 85.6% (95%CI 81.3, 89.0), with a higher acceptability among menopausal users compared to contraceptive ring users (94.4% vs. 83.7%, respectively).

In a recent 12-week RCT of 302 postmenopausal women with moderate to severe symptoms of vulvovaginal itching, pain, dryness, irritation, or pain with penetration, vaginal estrogen plus vaginal lubricant performed similarly to placebo plus lubricant with half the women in each group reporting a clinically significant drop in scores with treatment. Similarly, Aloe Vera cream performed as well as vaginal estrogen on vaginal atrophy symptoms and vaginal health index in an RCT of 60 women with atrophic vaginitis.

Ospemifene (oral selective estrogen-receptor modulator—estrogen agonist in vagina and estrogen antagonist in endometrium, progestogen not needed): 60 mg by mouth once daily. Not FDA-approved for women at high risk of breast cancer. Authors of a network meta-analysis including 44 controlled trials with 12,637 participants found no differences between ospemifene and other active therapies in most efficacy outcomes. Posttreatment endometrial thickness values were slightly increased but no cases of endometrial carcinoma or hyperplasia were reported.
Oxytocin was not found to be of benefit for GMS based on a meta-analysis of 7 studies with 631 patients.
Hyaluronic acid may be comparable to estrogen therapy and may be a good candidate for women who cannot use hormonal therapy.

Non-hormonal vaginal moisturizers and lubricants can be used for minor symptoms like vaginal dryness or sexual activity. Vaginal moisturizers are applied every few days to keep tissues hydrated, while vaginal lubricants are used during sexual activity

CO2 laser therapy has been used successfully in patients with GSM symptoms, although trial results are mixed. Vaginal laser therapy was superior to vaginal estrogen for GSM in a 2021 Bayesian network analysis of 29 randomized trials of 8311 patients, while another 2021 meta-analysis showed no difference between the two.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 25 studies including 1,152 patients demonstrated a significant reduction in symptoms in all studies in favor of CO2 laser therapy, although Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) scores reached a clinically-relevant level in only 2 studies. No major adverse events were reported.

Authors of another meta-analysis of 6 RCTs with 270 women with GSM randomized to laser therapy or vaginal estrogen therapy found similar improvement in genitourinary symptoms in the two treatment arms, as did a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs comparing laser to sham treatment of GMS, the latter also reporting improvement in patient satisfaction. However, in the most recent trial of laser vs. sham treatment, including 60 women with moderate to severe GMS, there were no differences in most bothersome symptom scores at 12 weeks.
Preparations and dosing: Information for patients on hormone therapy formulations is available on the FDA website.

Transdermal estrogen preparations are more expensive than oral preparations, and some women may choose oral estrogens based on lower cost, even though transdermal estrogens avoid the “first-pass” liver effect and consequent thromboembolic risk of oral estrogens.

Estrogen: All forms of systemic estrogen should be prescribed on a continuous, daily basis; unlike OCs, estrogen for MHT is NOT cycled. Standard-dose estrogen therapy: Estradiol, transdermal: 0.0375 to 0.075 mg per day Estradiol, oral: 1 mg once daily Conjugated equine estrogens (CEE): 0.625 mg once daily
High-dose estrogen therapy (post-oophorectomy, VMS starting at younger age): Estradiol, transdermal: 0.1 mg per day (or greater) Estradiol, oral: 2 mg once daily Conjugated equine estrogens (CEE): 1.25 to 2.5 mg once daily
Low-dose estrogen therapy (VMS milder or starting at older age): Estradiol, transdermal: 0.025 mg per day Estradiol, oral: 0.5 mg once daily Conjugated equine estrogens (CEE): 0.3 mg per dayUsually initiate therapy at standard doses and adjust as needed. It is unclear if lower doses are adequate to maintain bone density.

Progestogens: May be given cyclically (approximately 10 days every 1−4 months) or continuously (same dose every day). Cyclic progestin (with continuous daily estrogen) may be better for younger, perimenopausal women; while withdrawal bleeding may continue for several years, cyclic progestin administration at least minimizes irregular bleeding. Continuous progestin (with continuous daily estrogen) may be a better choice later in menopause, when the endometrium is atrophic and bleeding is minimal. Progestogen doses: Oral micronized progesterone (cyclic): 200 mg once daily for 10 to 14 days every 1 to 4 months Oral micronized progesterone (continuous): 100 mg once daily Medroxyprogesterone acetate/MPA (cyclic): 5 to10 mg once daily for 10 days every 1 to 4 months
“Bioidentical” hormones: There is no evidence of better safety profile than standard therapies and there are concerns about consistency and purity of preparations.

“Custom compounded” hormones have no advantages over FDA-approved prescription products; inform patients that standard formulations are, in fact, “bioidentical.” ACOG consensus statement advises clinicians to counsel patients that FDA-approved MHTs are recommended for the management of menopausal symptoms over compounded bioidentical MHT. For patients requesting these therapies, clinicians should educate them on the lack of FDA approval of these preparations and their potential risks and benefits, including the risks specific to compounding outlined in this reference.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 29 RCTs including 1,808 peri- and postmenopausal patients found compounded bioidentical hormone therapy, used primarily in short-term RCTs, was not associated with adverse changes in lipid profile or glucose metabolism. Vaginal androgens in these preparations appears beneficial for vaginal atrophy symptoms. However, data from these trials are insufficient to assess clinical risk of breast or endometrial cancer and cardiovascular disease.

Progestogen for prevention of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer: Women with a uterus must be prescribed EPT to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Women with a hysterectomy or women receiving only low-dose vaginal estrogen do not need a progestogen and may be prescribed estrogen-only therapy (ET). Consider micronized progesterone rather than synthetic progestins to minimize breast cancer risk.
A 2024 review listed complementary and alternative therapies that have been tried for genitourinary symptoms of menopause, without providing information on effectiveness.

Cognitive−behavioral therapy (CBT) Authors of a meta-analysis of 14 RCTs including 1618 patients found CBT superior to control groups for reducing hot flushes (SMD expressed as Hedge’s g 0.4, 95% CI 0.2-0.6, I2 = 45), night sweats, depression (g 0.5, 95% CI 0.3-0.7, I2 = 51), anxiety (g = 0.4, 95% CI 0.2-0.5, I2 = 49), and fatigue, and improving quality of life. Improved sleep has also been reported.
Clinical hypnosis

Mindfulness-based stress reduction Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 trials of mindfulness training or CBT demonstrated short-term (<20 weeks) benefit over placebo for reduced menopausal symptoms and hot-flash bother; reduction in hot-flash bother lasted beyond 20 weeks. In another meta-analysis of 5 studies, mindfulness training for menopausal patients improved sleep quality score (SMD -1.4, 95% CI -2.4 to -0.5) and perceived stress score (MD -4.2, 95% CI -6.4 to -2.0) compared to controls.
Melatonin-fluoxetine (not melatonin alone) benefit sleep disturbances due to VSM (meta-analysis of 43 RCTs and 32,271 women).

Black cohosh alone or in combination with St. John's wort improves neurovegetative and psychological menopausal symptoms based on a 2021 meta-analysis,, and a 2017 meta-analysis found black cohosh better than placebo for hot flases. In the most recent meta-analysis of 22 papers with 2310 patients, black cohosh extract was associated with significant improvements in overall menopausal symptoms, hot flashes, and somatic symptoms compared with placebo. Black cohosh did not significantly improve anxiety or depressive symptoms

Acupuncture. A 2021 review of 17 studies involving 1,123 participants showed that electro-acupuncture (EA) had higher efficacy than traditional acupuncture, significantly higher than sham acupuncture, and comparable to SSRI/SNRI and neuroleptic agents for treating hot flashes. EA and MHT did not differ in effectiveness or ratings on the Kupperman index, an 11-item menopausal symptom questionnaire in a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs including 746 patients, although risk of bias and clinical/statistical heterogeneity limited the ability to draw firm conclusions.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs including 1784 patients comparing acupuncture with sham acupuncture did not find a decrease in hot flash frequency or severity, although increases in E2 and decreases in FSH and LH, similar to MHT, were observed.
Among women with breast cancer, improvement in VMS was greater among patients treated with acupuncture than among those treated with sham acupuncture or untreated control patients
Recommended with caution (incomplete or weak evidence of efficacy):
Weight loss

Soy isoflavones—there is inconclusive evidence that phytoestrogens reduce the frequency or severity of hot flushes and night sweats in perimenopausal or postmenopausal women; a strong placebo effect was noted in most trials, with a reduction in frequency ranging from 1% to 59% with placebo. However, authors of a recent systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that isoflavones were better than placebo for hot flashes. Based on a systematic review and meta-analysis, authors concluded that isoflavone treatment, primarily isoflavone glycosides, improve bone mineral density over placebo. No data on fracture reduction were presented.

Ginseng may be helpful for reducing menopausal symptoms, hot flashes and quality-of-life scores based on a meta-analysis of 3 studies, but did not prove beneficial for sexual function; study bias was reported as a concern.

Yoga, practiced for 20 weeks, was shown to reduce menopausal symptoms measured by the Menopause Rating Scale and improve sleep quality for menopausal women over the control group based on an RCT with 208 patients; symptoms but not sleep quality were improved for perimenopausal women in the trial.
Stellate ganglion block
Not recommended (negative or insufficient evidence of efficacy):
Cooling techniques
Avoidance of triggers
Paced respiration
Relaxation therapy

OTC supplements and herbal remedies—very little high-quality scientific evidence regarding the effectiveness and long-term safety of herbal preparations and hormones including black cohosh, dong quai root, kava, flax, or licorice
Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) supplementation for cognition or GMS
Calibration of neural oscillations
Chiropractic interventions
Aromatherapy

Lifestyle modifications including adequate sleep, regular exercise, healthy diet, relaxation, and exercises are useful adjuncts and are often adequate by themselves for menopausal symptom relief, but there is no evidence that they are any more effective than placebo for moderately severe hot flashes.

The act of monitoring symptoms by keeping a diary may reduce physical symptoms and negative emotions; in an RCT including 100 peri and postmenopausal women, the monitoring-intervention group reported a 42% reduction in physical symptoms at 2-week follow-up vs. a 12% reduction in the control group and significantly reduced negative emotions which did not change for the control group.

A dietary intervention consisting of a plant-based diet, minimizing oils, plus daily soybeans for 12 weeks significantly reduced the frequency (88% decrease vs. 34% for controls) and severity of postmenopausal hot flashes in an RCT with 84 symptomatic postmenopausal women. Overall, nutritional interventions are not well studied.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 21 RCTs including 2884 participants found no difference comparing exercise to no-treatment control in vasomotor frequency, but exercise significantly improved severity of vasomotor symptoms (10 studies, SMD 0.25, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.47, very low certainty of evidence). However, the effect size was no longer significant when studies with a high risk of bias were excluded (SMD 0.11, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.26). Sleep, however, may be improved.

An RCT including 125 post-menopausal women found those randomized to 12-week Qigong exercises vs. controls had significant improvement in menopausal symptom severity at the somatic, psychological, and urogenital levels, as well as in the total Menopause Rating Scale score.

Exercise has a small statistically significant and potentially important effect on maintaining bone density in postmenopausal women compared to control groups, but there appears to be no fracture benefit. A meta-analysis of walking as exercise therapy confirmed positive effects on femoral neck bone density, but not spine BMD with interventions of more than 6 months.

While some guidelines discuss continued MHT in terms of “lowest dose for the shortest time,” this is based on weak evidence. Many women have menopausal symptoms for a decade or longer, and for women who are appropriately selected, the benefits of ongoing MHT may outweigh the risks. It is generally safe to continue MHT at whatever dose and for however long is necessary. Use informed decision-making after reviewing a woman’s symptoms and risks.
Discontinuing MHT results in recurrence of hot flashes in about half of women.

While providers should not stop MHT arbitrarily, it is reasonable to periodically decrease or taper the prescribed dose to see if it is still required. Several guidelines suggest a strategy of assuring women that they will be able to resume their previous dose of MHT without the necessity of a return visit.
Very little data exist to guide discontinuing MHT in long-term users, but tapering MHT (decreasing dosage and/or increasing intervals) over a few months is reasonable.

Oral contraceptive pills (OCs)—these have far more potent estrogenic effects (roughly 4−5 times the dose) than standard MHT; continuing OCs during the perimenopause should not be considered “safer” or seen as a substitute for shared decision-making regarding MHT.
Rapid and significant bone loss may occur after surgical menopause or after discontinuation of MHT.
Fluid retention, bloating, headache: may be either estrogenic or progestin side effects; try modifying progestogen first. Micronized progesterone is usually better tolerated than MPA.

Bleeding while on continuous estrogen/sequential progestin MHT: withdrawal bleeding may continue for several years; irregular spotting usually resolves within a few months. Consider increasing progestogen dose (especially if proliferative endometrium is found on sampling).

Bleeding while on continuous estrogen/continuous progestin MHT is usually due to unstable atrophic endometrium; increase progestogen or add levonorgestrel IUD. Levonorgestrel IUD or vaginal progesterone suppositories minimize systemic absorption while still providing adequate endometrial protection.
Weight gain or redistribution (increased abdominal fat) is not caused or prevented by MHT.

Many women have troublesome menopause symptoms for a decade or longer; in average-risk women requiring MHT, it is generally safe to continue treatment at whatever dose and for however long is necessary.
Many women have milder symptoms for shorter duration; they often need only reassurance and support.

Age at menopause was found to be inversely associated with subsequent frailty in a study of older Canadian women. With every year of menopause onset from age 30 years to 55 years or later, the frailty index decreased by 1.2% of the mean. The odds for being classified as frail using Fried's frailty phenotype model criteria were highest for women with menopause at ages 30-39 years (OR 1.33, 95% CI 0.72−2.27).

This finding was confirmed using data from 3 cross-sectional studies on age at menopause among community-dwelling women, with later onset of menopause being associated with lower risk of frailty. Based on these data, with each one-year increase in age at menopause there is a 2% decreased risk of prevalent frailty (pooled odds ratio [OR] 0.98, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.96-0.99). Surgical menopause did not predict incident frailty based on 2 studies.
Premature menopause is associated with increased risk of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.
GSM is progressive, sometimes with irreversible changes; these can be minimized with treatment.

Many women have troublesome menopause symptoms for a decade or longer; in average-risk women requiring MHT, it is generally safe to continue MHT at an effective dose for however long is necessary. Up to 10% of women continue to report symptoms for 12 years after their final menstrual period.
Many women have milder symptoms for shorter duration; they often need only reassurance and support.
Provide support and encouragement, through accessibility and close follow-up, for women who have initiated MHT.
Regularly evaluate each woman's ongoing need for MHT to dertermine if it can be discontinued or if a lower dose is sufficient for symptom relief.
Be aware of changes in our understanding and in standards of care associated with MHT.

Before starting MHT, each patient should be evaluated for cardiovascular and breast cancer risk factors, and engage in a process of shared decision-making to help them decide on the most appropriate therapy for menopausal symptoms.

In younger patients (within the first 5−10 years of menopausal transition, less than age 60 years) who do not have any excess risk for breast cancer or CVD (especially those without a uterus who do not require a progestogen), the benefits of MHT may outweigh its very small absolute risks.

For women with prior breast cancer, data are conflicting on the safety of use of MHT with respect to breast cancer risk; no mortality differences have been reported. The HABITS RCT of women with prior breast cancer was stopped early at a median follow-up of 2.1 years due to an increased risk for recurrent breast cancer (hazard ratio [HR] 3.3, 95% CI 1.5−7.4). Of the original 447 women, 442 women were followed for a median of 4 years; 39 of the 221 women in the MHT arm and 17 of the 221 women in the control arm experienced a new breast cancer (HR 2.4, 95% CI 1.3−4.2). In the Stockholm RCT, 188 women were randomized to MHT and 190 to no MHT. This trial was also stopped early based on results of HABITS although no increased risk of breast cancer recurrence was seen at a median follow-up of 4.1 years (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.35−1.9). At 10-year follow-up of these women, 60 in the original HRT group and 48 among controls had a new breast cancer event (HR 1.3, 95% CI 0.9−1.9). However, there was a higher risk of contralateral breast cancer - 14 in the HRT group and 4 in the control group (HR 3.6; 95% CI 1.2−10.9). The lack of an observed difference in breast cancer events in this trial may have been due to lower exposure to progesterone for some women who used a regimen of medroxyprogesterone acetate for only 14 days every 3 months, fewer women who were node-positive compared to the HABITS trial (16% vs. 26%), and more women included who were undergoing tamoxifen therapy (52% vs 21%). In a epidemiologic modeling study, authors estimated that for women with a 'strong' family history taking no MHT, the cumulative breast cancer risk is 19.6% (age 50-80 years) and risk of dying from breast cancer is 3.2%. With 5 years' exposure to MHT (age 50-55 years), the model showed risk increased to 22.4% and 3.5%, respectively.
Many women have troublesome menopause symptoms for a decade or longer; it is generally safe to continue MHT at whatever dose and for however long is necessary.
Sexual function can be preserved and vaginal health maintained with regular sexual activity or other vaginal stimulation and use of moisturizers and lubricants as needed.

feature.caption: Hormone Therapy (HT) Risks in Women ages 50–59.
feature.feature_body:
In younger women (within the first 5–10 years of menopausal transition, less than age 60) who do not have any excess risk for breast cancer or cardiovascular disease, the benefits of MHT generally outweigh its very small absolute risks (breast cancer and venous thromboembolic events being of greatest concern). In subgroup analyses, the only significantly increased risk was for venous thromboembolism in women taking combined continuous MHT. However, other risks cannot be completely excluded as studies with enough power to detect differences within 10 years of menopause have not been done. Venous thromboembolism (VTE) and stroke Oral MHT increases the risk of deep venous thrombosis (CEE: 3/1000 per 5 years, HR 1.66 (0.76–3.67), CEE+MPA: 6/1000 per 5 years, HR 3.01 (1.36–6.66). Oral MHT increases the risk of pulmonary embolism (CEE: 2/1000 per 5 years, HR 1.53 (0.63–3.75), CEE+MPA: 3/1000 per 5 years, HR 1.53 (0.63–3.75). Some forms of progestogens may increase VTE risk. Transdermal estrogen, in observational studies, does not increase VTE risk (crude and imprecise ORs ranging from 0.87 to 1.16): nonoral routes of ET are strongly recommended, particularly for women with increased VTE risk. Breast cancer There is a small increased risk of breast cancer with (approximately 1–2 excess cases/1000 women per year with estrogen–progestogen MHT; NNTH at 1 year = 1000–1250 women, NNTH at 5 years = 200–250). Any increased risk appears to be seen only with synthetic progestins (e.g., medroxyprogesterone acetate) but not with oral micronized progesterone.
Cardiovascular disease Estrogen-only therapy (ET) started within the first 10 years of menopause may confer a modest benefit with lower CVD mortality (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.52–0.95; moderate quality evidence) and coronary heart disease (composite of death from cardiovascular causes and non-fatal myocardial infarction) (RR 0.52; 95% CI 0.29–0.96; moderate quality evidence). Estrogen started more than 10 years after menopause, after disease has become established; increases CVD risk, primarily due to thromboembolic risks, particularly oral ET (NNTH at 1 year = 1429 women). Transdermal estrogen does not adversely affect cardiovascular markers and is associated with a lower risk of myocardial infarction.
Gallbladder disease The risk of symptomatic gallbladder disease in menopausal women on MHT is approximately doubled after 5 to 7 years of use, but the absolute risk is small, increasing from 2.5/1000 women to 4.5/1000 women.
Endometrial cancer The use of unopposed estrogen in women with an intact uterus increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Adding a progestogen to estrogen (EPT) in women with an intact uterus prevents endometrial hyperplasia; the risk of endometrial hyperplasia with low-dose estrogen continuously combined with a minimum of 1 mg norethisterone acetate (NETA) or 1.5 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) was not significantly different from placebo (1 mg NETA: OR 0.04; 95% CI 0–0.28; 1.5 mg MPA: no hyperplasia events).
Stroke MHT may increase stroke risk, at 6/1000 women (NNTH) = 165; mean length of follow-up: 4.21 years (range: 2.0–7.1)). Stroke risk was greatest for women initiating MHT >10 years from menopause (RR 1.21; 95% CI 1.06–1.38). The risk of stroke with transdermal estrogen is less than that with oral estrogen.
Urinary stress and urge incontinence Urinary incontinence may be worsened with systemic MHT using CEE, with both estrogen-only (RR 1.32; 95% CI 1.17–1.48) as well as CEE combined with progestin (RR 1.11; 95% CI 1.04–1.18).
